masteryZone.q: Which Article of the Constitution grants Parliament the power to amend the Constitution?
opts: Article 356
Article 360
Article 368
Article 370
masteryZone.sol: Article 368 in Part XX of the Indian Constitution vests the amending power in Parliament.

masteryZone.q: A constitutional amendment bill can be introduced by:
opts: A Minister only
A Private Member only
Either a Minister or a Private Member
The President of India only
masteryZone.sol: The bill can be introduced by either a minister or a private member, without requiring prior presidential consent.

masteryZone.q: What majority is required in each House of Parliament to pass a constitutional amendment bill?
opts: Simple majority of members present and voting
Special majority (majority of total membership and 2/3 of members present and voting)
Absolute majority of total membership
Three-fourths majority of members present and voting
masteryZone.sol: Under Article 368, each House must pass the bill by a majority of its total membership and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.

masteryZone.q: In case of a deadlock between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on an amendment bill, what is the procedure?
opts: A joint sitting is summoned by the President.
The bill is referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
There is no provision for a joint sitting, and the bill falls.
The Lok Sabha passes the bill again to override the Rajya Sabha.
masteryZone.sol: There is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve disagreements on constitutional amendment bills. The bill simply falls.

masteryZone.q: The President's assent to a constitutional amendment bill was made obligatory by which amendment?
opts: 24th Amendment Act, 1971
42nd Amendment Act, 1976
44th Amendment Act, 1978
86th Amendment Act, 2002
masteryZone.sol: The 24th Amendment Act of 1971 made it mandatory for the President to give his assent to a constitutional amendment bill.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following are correct regarding the introduction of a constitutional amendment bill? (Select all that apply)
opts: It can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
It can be introduced in state legislatures.
It requires the prior recommendation of the President.
It can be introduced by a private member.
masteryZone.sol: An amendment bill can only be introduced in either House of Parliament (not state legislatures), does not require the President's prior recommendation, and can be introduced by a private member.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statements are correct about the special majority under Article 368? (Select all that apply)
opts: It requires a majority of the total membership of the House.
It requires a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
Total membership includes vacancies and absentees.
It is the same as the majority required to pass ordinary bills.
masteryZone.sol: The special majority requires both a majority of the total membership (which includes vacancies/absentees) and 2/3 of those present and voting. Ordinary bills only require a simple majority.

masteryZone.q: What are the limitations on the President's powers regarding a constitutional amendment bill passed by Parliament? (Select all that apply)
opts: The President cannot withhold assent.
The President cannot return the bill for reconsideration.
The President can veto the bill using suspense veto.
The President must give assent to the bill.
masteryZone.sol: The President must give assent, cannot withhold assent, and cannot return the bill. Suspense or absolute veto cannot be used.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following are NOT permitted under the procedure of Article 368? (Select all that apply)
opts: Joint sitting of the two Houses
Initiation of the amendment bill in a State Assembly
Prior recommendation of the President
Introduction of the bill by a Minister
masteryZone.sol: Joint sittings, state legislature initiation, and prior recommendation of the President are not permitted/required under Article 368. Ministers are permitted to introduce the bill.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following bodies are directly involved in passing a constitutional amendment bill? (Select all that apply)
opts: Lok Sabha
Rajya Sabha
State Legislatures (for federal provisions)
The Supreme Court of India
masteryZone.sol: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha pass the bill, and state legislatures ratify it if federal provisions are affected. The Supreme Court is not part of the passing process (though it can review it later).

masteryZone.q: A constitutional amendment bill can be initiated in a state legislature.
masteryZone.sol: No, only Parliament can initiate a constitutional amendment bill.

masteryZone.q: The President can return a constitutional amendment bill to Parliament for reconsideration.
masteryZone.sol: The President must give assent and cannot return the bill.

masteryZone.q: There is no provision for a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament in case of deadlock over an amendment bill.
masteryZone.sol: Article 368 does not provide for a joint sitting; each House must pass it separately.

masteryZone.q: The 24th Amendment Act of 1971 made it obligatory for the President to sign amendment bills.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, the 24th Amendment amended Article 368 to make presidential assent mandatory.

masteryZone.q: A private member of Parliament cannot introduce a constitutional amendment bill.
masteryZone.sol: Private members are allowed to introduce constitutional amendment bills.

masteryZone.q: Prior recommendation of the President is necessary before introducing an amendment bill.
masteryZone.sol: No prior recommendation of the President is required.

masteryZone.q: The term 'total membership' of a House includes vacancies and absentees.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, total membership refers to the total number of seats in the House, irrespective of vacancies.

masteryZone.q: The procedure for amending the Indian Constitution is a blend of rigidity and flexibility.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, some provisions can be amended by a simple majority, while others require special majorities or state ratifications.

masteryZone.q: The procedure for constitutional amendment is described in Article _______ of the Constitution.
masteryZone.sol: Article 368 describes the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure for it.

masteryZone.q: Constitutional amendment is dealt with in Part _______ of the Indian Constitution.
masteryZone.sol: Part XX containing Article 368 is dedicated to the amendment of the Constitution.

masteryZone.q: The 24th Amendment Act was passed in the year _______ to make presidential assent mandatory.
masteryZone.sol: The 24th Amendment was enacted in 1971.

masteryZone.q: An amendment bill must be passed by each House of Parliament by a _______ majority.
masteryZone.sol: A special majority is required under Article 368.

masteryZone.q: In case of disagreement between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, there is no provision for a _______ sitting.
masteryZone.sol: No joint sitting can be held for an amendment bill.

masteryZone.q: If a federal provision is to be amended, it must be ratified by the legislatures of at least _______ of the states.
masteryZone.sol: Federal amendments require ratification by at least half of the states.

masteryZone.q: State legislatures ratify a federal amendment bill by a _______ majority.
masteryZone.sol: Ratification by states requires a simple majority of members present and voting.

masteryZone.q: The power to initiate an amendment bill lies exclusively with the _______.
masteryZone.sol: State legislatures cannot initiate a constitutional amendment bill; only Parliament can.

masteryZone.q: Match the procedural features with their descriptions:

options.text: A. Constitutional amendment power and procedure
B. Mandatory presidential assent to amendment bills
C. Consequence of disagreement between Houses (bill falls)

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the stages of an amendment bill with their characteristics:

B. Special majority in each House separately

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the majorities required under Article 368 with their definitions:

options.text: A. More than 50% of the total seats in the House
B. Not less than two-thirds (2/3) of those voting
C. Simple majority of members present and voting in state assemblies

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.sol: In either House of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha).

masteryZone.sol: No, it is not required.

masteryZone.q: Can a private member of Parliament introduce a constitutional amendment bill?
masteryZone.sol: Yes, they can.

masteryZone.q: Can the President veto or return a constitutional amendment bill for reconsideration?
masteryZone.sol: No, the President must give assent to the bill.

masteryZone.q: Which constitutional amendment act took away the President's power to withhold assent to amendment bills?
masteryZone.sol: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971.

masteryZone.q: What happens to a constitutional amendment bill if it is rejected by the Rajya Sabha?
masteryZone.sol: The bill falls and cannot be passed (there is no joint sitting).

masteryZone.q: Does the Constitution prescribe a time limit for states to ratify a federal amendment bill?
masteryZone.sol: No, there is no time limit prescribed.

masteryZone.sol: Part XX of the Constitution.

masteryZone.q:

2. It requires the prior recommendation of the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because no prior recommendation is required.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. In case of disagreement on a constitutional amendment bill, the President can summon a joint sitting of both Houses.
2. The President can withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are incorrect. There is no joint sitting provision, and the President cannot withhold assent.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the special majority under Article 368:
1. It requires a majority of the total membership of each House.
2. It requires a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting in each House.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct, as they outline the dual requirement of the special majority under Article 368.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 24th Amendment Act of 1971 insulated constitutional amendments from Article 13.
2. Article 368 was amended to make the President's assent obligatory.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct. The 24th Amendment added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3) and made the assent mandatory.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. State legislatures can initiate a constitutional amendment by passing a resolution with a special majority.
2. The state legislatures must ratify federal amendment bills by a special majority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are incorrect. States cannot initiate amendments, and they ratify federal amendments by a simple majority, not a special majority.

masteryZone.q: Why is there no provision for a joint sitting in the case of a constitutional amendment bill?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure that both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha have equal voice and veto power on altering the Constitution. A joint sitting would allow the larger Lok Sabha to easily override the Rajya Sabha, undermining the federal balance and the bicameral principle.

masteryZone.q: Why was the President's power to veto or return a constitutional amendment bill removed by the 24th Amendment in 1971?
masteryZone.sol: To establish that the constituent power of Parliament is supreme and cannot be blocked by the executive (represented by the President acting on the advice of the Cabinet). This ensured that once the elected representatives pass a constitutional amendment, it must become law.

masteryZone.q: Why is prior recommendation of the President not required for introducing a constitutional amendment bill?
masteryZone.sol: Because amending the Constitution is a constituent function of the legislature, not an ordinary legislative or financial function. Thus, the parliament is allowed to initiate the process without executive pre-clearance.

masteryZone.q: How is a disagreement between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha on a constitutional amendment bill resolved?
masteryZone.sol: It cannot be resolved. Unlike ordinary bills, there is no provision for a joint sitting. If either House rejects the bill or refuses to pass it with the required special majority, the bill simply dies and falls.

masteryZone.q: How does the calculation of 'majority of total membership' work under Article 368?
masteryZone.sol: It is calculated based on the total number of seats in the House as prescribed by law, regardless of any current vacancies, absentees, or members suspended. For example, in a House of 543 seats, the majority of total membership is always 272, even if 20 seats are vacant.

masteryZone.q: How did the 24th Amendment Act, 1971, change the relationship between Article 13 and Article 368?
masteryZone.sol: It added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), declaring that nothing in Article 13 (which voids laws violating Fundamental Rights) shall apply to any amendment made under Article 368. This was designed to shield constitutional amendments from judicial review based on Fundamental Rights.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: A constitutional amendment bill is introduced in the Lok Sabha by a private member and is passed with a special majority. However, when it goes to the Rajya Sabha, it is rejected. Can the Prime Minister request the President to summon a joint session? What is the outcome of the bill?
masteryZone.sol: No, the Prime Minister cannot request a joint session because Article 368 does not permit joint sittings for constitutional amendments. As the Rajya Sabha rejected the bill, the bill immediately falls and is dead.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: In 1971, Parliament passed a bill that sought to amend Article 368 itself. The bill was passed by a special majority in both Houses and sent directly to the President for assent. The President's office points out that since the bill amends Article 368 (a federal feature), it was not sent to the states. Is the President correct in withholding assent?
masteryZone.sol: Yes, the President's office is correct. Since Article 368 is a federal provision, any amendment to it must first be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the states before being presented to the President. Without state ratification, the bill is invalid and cannot be signed.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: During a vote on a constitutional amendment bill in the Lok Sabha, out of 543 seats, 40 seats are vacant and 103 members are absent. 400 members are present and voting. 268 members vote 'Yes' and 132 vote 'No'. Does the bill pass the Lok Sabha? Explain.
masteryZone.sol: No, the bill does not pass. Although 268 is more than two-thirds of the 400 members present and voting (2/3 of 400 is 267), it fails the second condition: it must be supported by a majority of the total membership of the House (543 seats). The majority of 543 is 272. Since 268 is less than 272, the bill fails.

masteryZone.q: Explain the step-by-step procedure for passing a constitutional amendment bill under Article 368 to a classmate.
masteryZone.sol:
1. Introduction: The bill can be introduced in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha by a minister or private member (no prior presidential consent needed).
2. Passage in Parliament: It must be passed by each House separately by a special majority (majority of total seats + 2/3 of members present and voting).
3. State Ratification (if federal): If it affects federal features (like SC, HC, lists), it must be ratified by at least half the state legislatures by a simple majority.
4. Presidential Assent: The bill is presented to the President, who must sign it. The President cannot veto or return it.

masteryZone.q: Explain why the Indian amendment procedure is described as a 'unique synthesis of rigidity and flexibility'.
masteryZone.sol: It is flexible because some administrative provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (like an ordinary law). It is rigid because most core provisions (Fundamental Rights, DPSP) require a special majority under Article 368. Furthermore, federal provisions are extremely rigid, requiring the consent of at least half the state legislatures in addition to a special majority in Parliament.

masteryZone.q: Explain the difference between a Minister and a Private Member introducing a constitutional amendment bill.
masteryZone.sol: A Minister introduces a government bill, which represents the official policy of the ruling party. A Private Member is any MP who is not a minister. Both are legally permitted to introduce a constitutional amendment bill, and both bills must follow the exact same strict procedure (special majority in each house) to pass, meaning private member amendment bills rarely pass due to lack of ruling majority support.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament?
opts: Fundamental Rights
Directive Principles of State Policy
Abolition or creation of legislative councils in states
Election of the President and its manner
masteryZone.sol: Abolition or creation of legislative councils in states (Article 169) is amended by a simple majority of Parliament and is outside the scope of Article 368.

masteryZone.q: How many states must ratify a constitutional amendment bill affecting federal provisions?
opts: All of the states
At least half of the states
Two-thirds of the states
Three-fourths of the states
masteryZone.sol: If the bill seeks to amend federal provisions, it must be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the states.

masteryZone.q: The landmark doctrine of 'Basic Structure' was introduced by the Supreme Court in which year?
masteryZone.sol: The 'Basic Structure' doctrine was introduced in the Kesavananda Bharati case on April 24, 1973.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the 'Basic Structure' of the Indian Constitution?
opts: Judicial Review
Sovereign, democratic and republican structure
The absolute power of Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution
Rule of Law
masteryZone.sol: Parliament does not have absolute power to amend the Constitution; its power is limited by the Basic Structure doctrine. This limitation itself is part of the basic structure.

masteryZone.q: Which amendment shifted the subjects of education and forests from the State List to the Concurrent List?
opts: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
44th Amendment Act, 1978
73rd Amendment Act, 1992
86th Amendment Act, 2002
masteryZone.sol: The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 transferred five subjects to the Concurrent List, including education and forests.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following provisions can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (outside Article 368)? (Select all that apply)
opts: Rules of procedure in Parliament
Official language of the Union
Fundamental Rights
Citizenship - acquisition and termination
masteryZone.sol: Rules of procedure, official language, and citizenship can be amended by a simple majority. Fundamental Rights require a special majority under Article 368.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following provisions require a special majority of Parliament and ratification by at least half of the states? (Select all that apply)
opts: Election of the President and its manner
Distribution of legislative powers between Union and States
Directive Principles of State Policy
Representation of states in Parliament
masteryZone.sol: Presidential election, distribution of legislative powers, and representation of states are federal features and require state ratification. DPSP only requires special majority under Article 368.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following have been declared by the Supreme Court as part of the 'Basic Structure'? (Select all that apply)
opts: Judicial Review
Secular character of the Constitution
Federal character of the Constitution
Free and fair elections
masteryZone.sol: All the listed features (judicial review, secularism, federalism, free and fair elections) have been declared by the Supreme Court as core components of the Basic Structure.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following are true about the state ratification of federal amendment bills? (Select all that apply)
opts: It requires a simple majority in the state legislatures.
It must be ratified by at least half of the states.
There is no time limit for states to ratify the bill.
It must be passed by state legislatures using a special majority.
masteryZone.sol: State ratification requires a simple majority in the legislatures of at least half the states, and no time limit is specified in the Constitution.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following cases are key milestones in the evolution of the amending power under Article 368? (Select all that apply)
opts: Shankari Prasad Case (1951)
Golak Nath Case (1967)
Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)
Minerva Mills Case (1980)
masteryZone.sol: All four cases are landmark judicial decisions that shaped the scope and limits of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution.

masteryZone.q: Amendments passed by a simple majority are not deemed to be amendments under Article 368.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, they are outside the scope of Article 368 and are passed like ordinary laws.

masteryZone.q: Parliament can amend the Fundamental Rights by a simple majority.
masteryZone.sol: Fundamental Rights require a special majority under Article 368.

masteryZone.q: State ratification of federal amendments requires a special majority in the state legislatures.
masteryZone.sol: No, it only requires a simple majority of members present and voting in state assemblies.

masteryZone.q: The Basic Structure doctrine was introduced in the Golak Nath case in 1967.
masteryZone.sol: It was introduced in the Kesavananda Bharati case in 1973.

masteryZone.q: Article 368 itself can be amended by Parliament.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, but since it is a federal feature, it requires a special majority plus ratification by at least half of the states.

masteryZone.q: The Preamble to the Indian Constitution cannot be amended.
masteryZone.sol: The Preamble was amended by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976 and is amendable, provided the basic structure is not altered.

masteryZone.q: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are open to challenge in court if they violate basic features.
masteryZone.sol: Yes, as held by the Supreme Court in the I.R. Coelho case (2007).

masteryZone.q: There is a six-month time limit within which states must ratify federal amendment bills.
masteryZone.sol: No time limit is prescribed in the Constitution for state ratification.

masteryZone.q: The Supreme Court introduced the Basic Structure doctrine on April 24, _______.
masteryZone.sol: The Kesavananda Bharati verdict was delivered on April 24, 1973.

masteryZone.q: Amendments passed by a simple majority are considered _______ the scope of Article 368.
masteryZone.sol: They are outside the scope of Article 368.

masteryZone.q: An amendment to the Seventh Schedule requires ratification by at least _______ of the states.
masteryZone.sol: Since the Seventh Schedule is federal, at least half the states must ratify it.

masteryZone.q: The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 is commonly known as the _______ Constitution.
masteryZone.sol: It is known as the Mini-Constitution due to its vast scope.

masteryZone.q: The Supreme Court case that reaffirmed the Basic Structure cut-off date as April 24, 1973, was the _______ case.
masteryZone.sol: The Waman Rao case (1981) confirmed this cut-off date.

masteryZone.q: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles require a _______ majority of Parliament to be amended.
masteryZone.sol: They require a special majority under Article 368.

masteryZone.q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced via the _______ Constitutional Amendment Act.
masteryZone.sol: The 101st Amendment Act of 2016 introduced GST.

masteryZone.q: The 103rd Amendment Act provided a 10% reservation for the _______ category.
masteryZone.sol: It provided reservation for the Economically Weaker Sections.

options.text: A. Simple majority of Parliament (outside Article 368)
B. Special majority of Parliament under Article 368
C. Special majority of Parliament and ratification by half of the states

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the cases with their major judicial declarations:

options.text: A. Fundamental Rights cannot be amended or abridged
B. Introduced the Basic Structure doctrine
C. Reaffirmed Basic Structure and struck down unlimited amending power

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the recent amendments with their key subjects:

options.text: A. Introduction of Goods and Services Tax (GST)
B. 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)
C. Restored state power to identify backward classes (SEBCs)

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Which judicial case established the 'Basic Structure' doctrine?
masteryZone.sol: The Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973).

masteryZone.q: Can Parliament amend the basic features of the Constitution?
masteryZone.sol: No, the basic structure cannot be altered or destroyed by any constitutional amendment.

masteryZone.q: Give one example of a provision that can be amended by a simple majority.
masteryZone.sol: Admission or establishment of new states (or rules of procedure in Parliament).

masteryZone.q: What majority is required in state legislatures for ratifying a federal amendment bill?
masteryZone.sol: A simple majority of members present and voting.

masteryZone.q: Is the Preamble of the Indian Constitution amendable?
masteryZone.sol: Yes, the Preamble can be amended under Article 368, provided it does not violate the basic structure.

masteryZone.q: Which amendment removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights?
masteryZone.sol: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978.

masteryZone.q: Which case clarified that all laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are subject to judicial review?
masteryZone.sol: The I.R. Coelho Case (2007).

masteryZone.q: Which amendment shifted 'Education' from the State List to the Concurrent List?
masteryZone.sol: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the types of amendments:
1. Amendments by a simple majority are outside the scope of Article 368.
2. Amendments under Article 368 require either a special majority or a special majority with state ratification.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct. The Constitution provides for three classes of amendments, only two of which fall under Article 368.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment Act of 1951.
2. Laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are completely immune to judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because laws added after the Kesavananda Bharati cut-off date (April 24, 1973) can be challenged if they violate the basic structure.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills case (1980) struck down sections of the 42nd Amendment that gave unlimited amending power to Parliament.
2. The Court held that a limited amending power is a basic feature of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct. The Minerva Mills case struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and declared the limited amending power as basic structure.

masteryZone.q:
Which of the following federal features require state ratification for their amendment?
1. Election of the President and its manner.
2. The Supreme Court and High Courts.
3. The distribution of legislative powers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
masteryZone.sol: All three are federal provisions and require a special majority of Parliament plus ratification by at least half of the states.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct, describing the key impacts of the 42nd and 44th amendments.

masteryZone.q: Why did the Supreme Court introduce the 'Basic Structure' doctrine in 1973?
masteryZone.sol: To prevent Parliament from using its amending power under Article 368 to completely destroy or rewrite the core democratic and federal character of the Constitution. It set a limit to ensure that Parliament, which is a creature of the Constitution, cannot destroy the instrument that created it.

masteryZone.q: Why do federal provisions of the Constitution require ratification by at least half of the states for amendment?
masteryZone.sol: To protect the federal balance of power between the Centre and the States. Since India is a 'Union of States', the central government cannot unilaterally change the division of powers, state representation, or judicial structures without securing consensus from at least half the states.

masteryZone.q: Why are some amendments, like the admission of new states, kept outside the scope of Article 368?
masteryZone.sol: To allow flexibility in everyday administrative and procedural matters. If every minor administrative change (like renaming a state or changing salaries of judges) required a special majority and state ratification under Article 368, it would lead to governance paralysis.

masteryZone.q: How does the Basic Structure doctrine act as a check on Parliament's constituent power?
masteryZone.sol: It gives the judiciary (the Supreme Court) the power of judicial review to examine any constitutional amendment. If the Court finds that an amendment destroys or alters a fundamental feature (like secularism, federalism, or judicial review), it can declare the amendment unconstitutional and void.

masteryZone.q: How can the Preamble of the Constitution be amended?
masteryZone.sol: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368 using a special majority, as long as the amendment does not destroy any basic features of the Preamble (like democracy, secularism, or republicanism). This was demonstrated when it was amended once in 1976.

masteryZone.q: How did the I.R. Coelho case (2007) clarify the judicial status of the Ninth Schedule?
masteryZone.sol: It ruled that the Ninth Schedule does not grant blank immunity. Any law placed in it after April 24, 1973, is subject to judicial review. If such a law violates Fundamental Rights that form part of the basic structure, the court can strike it down.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: In 2014, Parliament passed the 99th Constitutional Amendment to establish the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC). The bill was passed by a special majority and ratified by more than half of the states. Yet, in 2015, the Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional. Under what doctrine did the Court act? Explain.
masteryZone.sol: The Supreme Court acted under the 'Basic Structure' doctrine. It ruled that the NJAC violated the independence of the judiciary, which is a core component of the basic structure. Even though the procedure of Article 368 was fully followed, the amendment was void because it altered a basic feature.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: Parliament passes a law changing the official language of the Union. A citizen challenges this in court, arguing that the law was passed by a simple majority and did not follow the special majority procedure under Article 368. Will the court strike down the law? Explain.
masteryZone.sol: No, the court will not strike down the law. Changing the official language of the Union is one of the provisions that can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament (outside Article 368). The procedure under Article 368 does not apply to this provision, making the simple majority passage fully valid.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: A state legislature passes a land reform law in 1975 and gets it included in the Ninth Schedule to avoid challenges based on the Right to Property. In 2010, a petitioner challenges the law for violating the basic structure. Can the court hear this petition, or is the law fully protected by the Ninth Schedule?
masteryZone.sol: The court can hear the petition. Under the I.R. Coelho ruling (2007), laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, are not immune to judicial review. If the law violates the basic structure, it can be declared invalid.

masteryZone.q: Explain the concept of the 'Basic Structure' of the Indian Constitution to a beginner.
masteryZone.sol: The Basic Structure is the core identity or the 'soul' of the Constitution. It includes essential values like democracy, secularism, federalism, and the rule of law. The Supreme Court decided in 1973 that while Parliament can change many things in the Constitution, it cannot touch or destroy these core values, ensuring that the fundamental nature of the nation remains intact.

masteryZone.q: Explain the difference between amendments under Article 368 and amendments outside Article 368.
masteryZone.sol: Amendments under Article 368 require a special majority of Parliament (total seat majority + 2/3 voting majority) and sometimes state ratification. They deal with core matters like Fundamental Rights. Amendments outside Article 368 are passed by a simple majority (like ordinary laws) and deal with administrative matters, like forming new states or changing salaries.

masteryZone.q: Explain how the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) resolved the conflict between parliamentary sovereignty and judicial review.
masteryZone.sol: Before 1973, Parliament claimed it had unlimited power to amend the Constitution, while the Court held that Fundamental Rights couldn't be touched. The Kesavananda Bharati case found a middle ground: it upheld Parliament's right to amend any part of the Constitution (including Fundamental Rights), but created the 'Basic Structure' limit, preserving the Court's power to strike down amendments that destroy the core of the Constitution.
